\begin{center}
{\Large\textbf{Mixed models in R: math and syntax for nlme, lme4, and glmmTMB}}\\
NRES 746
\end{center}

All three packages maximize a likelihood (or a restricted likelihood)
with the random effects integrated out. Fit the same model in two of
them and you get the same log-likelihood: the code pairs below agreed
on simulated data, except where a fit was singular or a method
approximate. Each model is written first in math, then in R, so you can
translate in either direction.

## Notation

- $i$ indexes observations; $j$ a group (site, stand); $k$ a subgroup
  nested in $j$ (plot within site); $m$ a second, crossed grouping
  (observer); $t$ time.
- $j[i]$ is the group that observation $i$ belongs to (the same lookup
  as `site[i]` in R or Stan).
- $\beta$s are fixed effects. Random effects ($a_j$, $b_j$, $v_{jk}$,
  $w_m$) are Normal with mean 0 and independent of each other and of
  the residuals unless stated. $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)$ is the
  residual.
- Every package writes the fixed part the same way (`y ~ x` means
  $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$); the random part is where they differ.

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
\textbf{In the model} & \textbf{Math} & \textbf{lme4 / glmmTMB term} \\
\midrule
fixed intercept and slope & $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$ & \texttt{y \textasciitilde{} x} \\
random intercept & $+\,a_{j[i]}$, \ $a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$ & \texttt{(1 | site)} \\
correlated intercept and slope & $+\,a_{j[i]} + b_{j[i]}x_i$, \ $(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0}, G)$ & \texttt{(x | site)} \\
uncorrelated intercept and slope & same, with $\text{Cov}(a_j, b_j) = 0$ & \texttt{(x || site)} \ (numeric $x$) \\
nested groups & $+\,a_j + v_{jk}$ & \texttt{(1 | site/plot)} \\
crossed groups & $+\,a_{j[i]} + w_{m[i]}$ & \texttt{(1 | site) + (1 | obs)} \\
AR(1) errors in time & $\eta_t = \phi\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ & \texttt{ar1(yearf + 0 | plot)} \\
log link, Poisson counts & $y_i \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_i)$, \ $\log\lambda_i = \ldots$ & \texttt{family = poisson} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

## 1. Which package when

- **`glmmTMB`** is the most practical default. One syntax covers Normal,
  Poisson, binomial, negative binomial, beta, Tweedie and other
  families; zero inflation; variances that depend on covariates; AR(1)
  and spatial structures; and crossed random effects. Ecological data
  often start out looking Poisson and turn out overdispersed or
  autocorrelated, and here that means changing one argument rather than
  switching packages. Its defaults are ML fits and Wald tests and
  intervals; for profile intervals use `confint(fit, method = "profile")`
  (variance terms come out on the log SD scale, so exponentiate them).
- **`lme4`** (`lmer()`, `glmer()`) is the better choice for inference on
  Normal models with few groups: `lmer()` fits by REML, `lmerTest` and
  `pbkrtest` give small-sample (Satterthwaite, Kenward-Roger) tests, and
  `confint()` profiles the likelihood by default. It's the most widely
  used and documented, and its sparse-matrix methods handle very large
  Normal models with crossed effects. No residual correlation or unequal
  variances.
- **`nlme`** (`lme()`, `gls()`) has the richest menu of residual
  structures for Normal data (`corCAR1()`, `corSpher()`, `varPower()`,
  and more), and `gls()` fits them with no random effects at all.
  Slower, Normal responses only, and crossed random effects are awkward.
- **Bayesian** (`brms`, Stan): priors, small numbers of groups, or
  models none of these can write.

```
                        nlme           lme4                 glmmTMB
Responses               Normal         Normal; glmer: GLMs  many (NB, beta, Tweedie, ...)
Crossed random effects  awkward        yes                  yes
Residual correlation    correlation =  no                   ar1(), ou(), exp() terms
Unequal variances       weights =      no                   dispformula =
Zero inflation          no             no                   ziformula =
Default fit             REML           REML (glmer: ML)     ML
Speed on large data     slow           fast                 fast
Fixed-effect p-values   t tests        via lmerTest         Wald z
```

## 2. Random-effect structures

Write `d` for the data frame; `site`, `plot`, and `obs` (observer) are
factors and `x` is numeric.

**Random intercept.** Observation $i$ in site $j$:
$$y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$$
Two observations in the same site share $a_j$, so their covariance is
$\sigma_a^2$; observations in different sites are independent. Four
parameters: $\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_a, \sigma_e$.

```{r syntax-ri}
lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | site, data = d)
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)
```

**Correlated random intercept and slope.** Each site gets its own line:
$$y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + a_j) + (\beta_1 + b_j)\,x_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} a_j \\ b_j \end{pmatrix} \sim
\text{MVN}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\
G = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_a^2 & \rho_{ab}\sigma_a\sigma_b \\
\rho_{ab}\sigma_a\sigma_b & \sigma_b^2 \end{pmatrix}\right)$$
Six parameters: $\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_a, \sigma_b, \rho_{ab}, \sigma_e$.
`(x | site)` includes the intercept; `(0 + x | site)` would give a random
slope only.

```{r syntax-rs}
lme(y ~ x, random = ~ x | site, data = d)
lmer(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (x | site), data = d)
```

**Uncorrelated random intercept and slope.** The same model with
$\rho_{ab} = 0$, so $G$ is diagonal (five parameters). In `nlme`,
`pdDiag` means "positive-definite, diagonal" (`pdSymm`, the default, is
the general form). In `lme4`, `(x || site)` is shorthand for
`(1 | site) + (0 + x | site)`.

```{r syntax-uncorrelated}
lme(y ~ x, random = list(site = pdDiag(~ x)), data = d)
lmer(y ~ x + (x || site), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (x || site), data = d)          # or diag(x | site)
```

If `x` is a factor, `lme4`'s `||` still estimates correlations among the
factor's levels. For a diagonal $G$ with a factor, use
`diag(trt | site)` in `glmmTMB`, `pdDiag(~ trt)` in `nlme`, or numeric
indicator columns in `lme4`: `(1 + trtB + trtC || site)`.

**Nested groups.** Observation $i$ in plot $k$ within site $j$:
$$y_{ijk} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ijk} + a_j + v_{jk} + \varepsilon_{ijk},
\qquad a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2), \quad v_{jk} \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)$$
The plot effect carries both subscripts: plot 1 in site A is a
different plot from plot 1 in site B. `site/plot` expands to
`(1 | site) + (1 | site:plot)`, and `site:plot` is the $jk$ subscript.
The covariance between two observations is $\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_v^2$ in
the same plot, $\sigma_a^2$ in the same site but different plots, and 0
in different sites.

```{r syntax-nested}
lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | site/plot, data = d)
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site/plot), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | site/plot), data = d)
```

**Crossed groups.** Every observer visits several sites:
$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + a_{j[i]} + w_{m[i]} + \varepsilon_i,
\qquad a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2), \quad w_m \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)$$
Neither subscript is nested in the other. Two observations covary if
they share a site ($\sigma_a^2$), an observer ($\sigma_w^2$), or both, so
no ordering of the data splits $V$ into independent blocks.

```{r syntax-crossed}
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs), data = d)
d$all <- factor(1)   # nlme: one group holding everything, block-diagonal G (slow for large n)
lme(y ~ x, data = d,
    random = list(all = pdBlocked(list(pdIdent(~ 0 + site), pdIdent(~ 0 + obs)))))
```

## 3. Residual correlation and unequal variances

Here the error, $\eta$, is correlated instead of independent (not
available in `lme4`). In `glmmTMB`, correlation enters as a
random-effect term with one level per observation; `dispformula = ~0`
removes the separate residual variance so the term *is* the residual,
matching `nlme`.

**AR(1) errors in time.** Plot $j$ in year $t$:
$$y_{jt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{jt} + \eta_{jt}, \qquad
\eta_{jt} = \phi\,\eta_{j,t-1} + \varepsilon_{jt}, \qquad
\varepsilon_{jt} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)$$
Within a plot, $\text{Cor}(\eta_{js}, \eta_{jt}) = \phi^{|s-t|}$ and
$\text{Var}(\eta_{jt}) = \sigma_e^2/(1-\phi^2)$; plots are independent. No
random effects, so the model is all residual structure.

```{r syntax-ar1}
gls(y ~ x, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ year | plot), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + ar1(yearf + 0 | plot), dispformula = ~0, data = d)    # yearf <- factor(year)
```

**Random site intercept plus AR(1) within each plot.** Plot $k$ in site
$j$, year $t$:
$$y_{jkt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{jkt} + a_j + \eta_{jkt}, \qquad
a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2), \qquad \eta_{jkt} \text{ AR(1) within plot}$$
$V = \sigma_a^2 ZZ^T + \sigma_e^2 R$: the random intercept adds
$\sigma_a^2$ wherever two values share a site, and $R$ holds the AR(1)
correlations within each plot.

```{r syntax-ri-ar1}
lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | site, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ year | site/plot), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | site) + ar1(yearf + 0 | plot), dispformula = ~0, data = d)  # unique plot labels
```

**Gaps in time: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.** The continuous-time
version of AR(1) uses the actual times:
$$\text{Cor}(\eta_{js}, \eta_{jt}) = e^{-\theta|s - t|} = \phi^{|s-t|},
\qquad \phi = e^{-\theta}$$
so a two-year gap gets $\phi^2$. `glmmTMB`'s `ar1()` treats the
*observed* times as consecutive (a missing year counts as a lag of 1);
`ou()` with `numFactor()` times handles gaps. `nlme`'s `corAR1()`
handles gaps with integer times; `corCAR1()` takes non-integer times.

```{r syntax-ou}
gls(y ~ x, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ year | plot), data = d)      # handles gaps
glmmTMB(y ~ x + ou(tt + 0 | plot), dispformula = ~0, data = d)       # tt <- numFactor(year)
```

**Exponential spatial correlation.** Locations $i$ and $k$ in the same
site, a distance $d_{ik}$ apart:
$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \eta_i, \qquad
\text{Cor}(\eta_i, \eta_k) = e^{-d_{ik}/\ell}$$
where $\ell$ is the range: correlation falls to $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$ at
distance $\ell$.

```{r syntax-spatial}
gls(y ~ x, correlation = corExp(form = ~ east + north | site), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x + exp(pos + 0 | site), dispformula = ~0, data = d)     # pos <- numFactor(east, north)
```

**A separate residual variance for each treatment.**
$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\text{trt}[i]}\right)$$

```{r syntax-varident}
gls(y ~ x, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | trt), data = d)
glmmTMB(y ~ x, dispformula = ~ trt, data = d)
```

Other `nlme` options: `corCAR1()` (continuous time), `corCompSymm()`,
`corGaus()`, `corSpher()`; `varPower(form = ~ fitted(.))`,
`varExp(form = ~ x)`. Other `glmmTMB` options: `cs()` (compound
symmetry), `gau()`, `mat()` (Matern), `us()` and `diag()` for
random-effect covariances. See `?corClasses`, `?varClasses`, and
`vignette("covstruct", package = "glmmTMB")`.

## 4. Non-Normal responses (GLMMs)

A GLMM puts the random effects on the link scale, where they are
Normal, and uses a non-Normal distribution for each observation given
those effects. `nlme` fits none of these.

**Poisson counts.**
$$y_{ij} \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_{ij}), \qquad
\log \lambda_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j, \qquad
a_j \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$$

```{r syntax-poisson}
glmer(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = poisson, data = d)
glmmTMB(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = poisson, data = d)
```

**Successes $s$ out of $n$ trials.**
$$s_{ij} \sim \text{Binom}(n_{ij}, p_{ij}), \qquad
\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j$$

```{r syntax-binomial}
glmer(cbind(s, n - s) ~ x + (1 | site), family = binomial, data = d)
glmmTMB(cbind(s, n - s) ~ x + (1 | site), family = binomial, data = d)
```

**Overdispersed counts.** Three common choices:

- Negative binomial (`nbinom2`): $\text{Var}(y_{ij}) = \mu_{ij} + \mu_{ij}^2/\theta$
  with $\log\mu_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + a_j$. (`nbinom1`:
  $\text{Var} = \mu(1 + \phi)$.)
- Observation-level random effect: add $o_i \sim N(0, \sigma_o^2)$ to
  the Poisson's $\log\lambda$, one per observation (`obs_id` has a
  unique level for each row).
- Zero-inflated negative binomial: $y_{ij} = 0$ with probability $\pi$;
  otherwise $y_{ij}$ is negative binomial as above. `ziformula = ~ 1`
  means a constant $\pi$ (on the logit scale); `~ x` would let it vary.

```{r syntax-overdispersed}
glmer.nb(count ~ x + (1 | site), data = d)                   # slower, approximate
glmmTMB(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = nbinom2, data = d)
glmer(count ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs_id), family = poisson, data = d)
glmmTMB(count ~ x + (1 | site) + (1 | obs_id), family = poisson, data = d)
glmmTMB(count ~ x + (1 | site), family = nbinom2, ziformula = ~ 1, data = d)
# others: beta_family() for proportions in (0, 1), tweedie(), Gamma(link = "log"), ...
```

**Offsets for effort or area.** A count from a plot of area $A_i$:
$\log\lambda_i = \log A_i + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + a_{j[i]}$, so
$\lambda_i / A_i$ is the density. Add `+ offset(log(area))` to the
formula in any package.

## 5. Fitting options

```
                       nlme                    lme4                          glmmTMB
REML/ML (default 1st)  method = "REML" / "ML"  REML = TRUE / FALSE (lmer)    REML = FALSE / TRUE
GLMM integration       --                      Laplace; nAGQ = (one effect)  Laplace
Spot a bad fit         --                      isSingular(fit)               diagnose(fit)
```

Convergence warnings? Try another optimizer:

```{r convergence}
lme(..., control = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
lmer(..., control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
allFit(fit)                                   # refit an lme4 model with every optimizer and compare
glmmTMB(..., control = glmmTMBControl(optimizer = optim, optArgs = list(method = "BFGS")))
```

- REML gives less biased variance estimates. Use ML when comparing
  models with different fixed effects (by AIC or a likelihood ratio
  test). `lmer()` and `glmmTMB()` have different defaults, so their
  default fits of the same Normal model differ slightly.
- `anova(fit1, fit2)` gives a likelihood ratio test in all three.
  Testing a variance at zero puts it on a boundary, so that p-value is
  conservative (too large).
- A **singular fit** (a variance estimated at zero, or a correlation at
  $\pm 1$) means the data can't support that random-effect structure.
  Simplify it (drop the correlation, or the random slope) rather than
  trusting the estimates. Different packages may stop at slightly
  different points on such a flat surface.
- Center and rescale predictors before blaming the optimizer.

## 6. Getting results out

```
                      nlme                     lme4                        glmmTMB
Fixed effects         fixef(fit)               fixef(fit)                  fixef(fit)$cond
Group deviations      ranef(fit)               ranef(fit)                  ranef(fit)
Group coefficients    coef(fit)                coef(fit)                   coef(fit)
Variance components   VarCorr(fit)             VarCorr(fit)                VarCorr(fit)
Confidence intervals  intervals(fit)           confint(fit) (profile)      confint(fit) (Wald)
Mean predictions      predict(fit, level = 0)  predict(fit, re.form = NA)  predict(fit, re.form = NA)
GLMM response scale   --                       type = "response"           type = "response"
Simulate new data     --                       simulate(fit)               simulate(fit)
Residual checks       ACF(fit, resType = "n")  DHARMa (below)              DHARMa (below)
```

In the math: `fixef()` returns the $\beta$s; `ranef()` the predicted
$a_j$, $b_j$ (shrunk toward 0); `coef()` each group's
$\beta_0 + a_j$ and $\beta_1 + b_j$; `VarCorr()` the $\sigma$s and
$\rho_{ab}$.

- `summary()`, `logLik()`, `AIC()`, and `nobs()` work everywhere.
  Log-likelihoods are comparable across packages for the same data and
  the same estimation method (ML vs. REML).
- `glmmTMB` keeps separate parts for the mean (`$cond`), zero inflation
  (`$zi`), and dispersion (`$disp`).
- For GLMMs, ordinary residual plots are hard to read. The `DHARMa`
  package simulates from the fitted model and gives residuals that
  should be uniform if the model is right.
- `broom.mixed::tidy(fit)` returns a data frame of estimates from any of
  the three.

## 7. Things that trip people up

- **Names for the same thing.** The AR(1) coefficient $\phi$ is `Phi` in
  `nlme` and appears as a correlation labeled `(ar1)` in `glmmTMB`'s
  `VarCorr()`. With AR(1) errors, both report the SD of the total
  error, $\sigma_e/\sqrt{1-\phi^2}$, not the innovation SD $\sigma_e$.
- **Time and space in `glmmTMB`.** `ar1()` needs a factor of equally
  spaced times and treats the observed times as consecutive. Use `ou()`
  with `numFactor()` times when there are gaps.
- **Unique times.** Each `time | group` combination must appear once.
  Two observations in the same plot and year need an extra grouping
  level.
- **Factors.** Make grouping variables factors. `glmmTMB` time terms
  need a factor (`ar1()`) or `numFactor()` (`ou()`, `exp()`). A factor
  inside `||` doesn't give uncorrelated effects (section 2).
- **Nested labels.** If plots are numbered 1, 2, 3 within every site,
  `(1 | plot)` wrongly treats plot 1 at every site as one plot. Use
  `(1 | site/plot)` or give plots unique labels.
- **Missing values** stop `nlme` fits; add `na.action = na.omit`.
- **p-values.** `lmer()` reports none by design (the degrees of freedom
  are unclear). `lmerTest` adds approximate ones; with few groups,
  treat any of them as rough.
- **Few groups.** With fewer than about five levels, a random-effect
  variance is poorly estimated in every package. Consider fixed effects
  or a Bayesian fit with an informative prior.

**Learn more:** Bolker's GLMM FAQ,
<https://bbolker.github.io/mixedmodels-misc/glmmFAQ.html>; Bates et al.
(2015, *J. Stat. Software* 67(1)) for `lme4`; Brooks et al. (2017, *R
Journal* 9: 378-400) and the `glmmTMB` vignettes; Pinheiro and Bates
(2000), *Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS*; Zuur et al. (2009),
*Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R*.
